summary: Specifies the architecture for mobile email as described by the Open Mobile Alliance, using Internet mail protocols, and shows how it meets OMA requirements for its Mobile Email service. It reflects the work of the IETF LEMONADE working group. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the blueprint showing how ordinary email tools can be used to deliver email to phones, to match what mobile phone groups asked for.

questions: how does oma mobile email work with imap
subtitle: How ordinary Internet mail protocols map onto the Open Mobile Alliance's architecture for email on mobile devices.

tldr.problem: The Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) defined a Mobile Email (MEM) service with its own requirements and architecture, and it needed to be realized with Internet mail protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps the IETF LEMONADE architecture (extended IMAP stores, extended SUBMIT servers and out-of-band notifications) onto the OMA MEM logical architecture, and shows how non-LEMONADE and non-IMAP back ends can be fronted.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational description of how the LEMONADE work meets OMA's requirements. It also names four categories of filters and flags security risks that are left to other documents.

today: RFC 5442 is an Informational RFC and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the LEMONADE profile as of March 2009, and its text refers to the OMA technical specification as ongoing work.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes the architecture of OMA Mobile Email (MEM) using Internet mail protocols defined by the IETF. The LEMONADE working group enhanced many of those protocols for the mobile environment, and the LEMONADE profile (RFC 4550 and its revision) summarizes them.

The RFC shows how three OMA documents, the MEM requirements, architecture and technical specification, relate to LEMONADE work in the IETF. It was extracted from sections of the profile revision and of the LEMONADE notifications document.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone companies wrote down what they wanted from email on a phone. This memo shows how normal email tools can do it.

sections.title: The OMA MEM Architecture
sections.content:
OMA's logical architecture has a MEM client (the user experience, which also stores mail to send while disconnected), a MEM server, and the MEM protocol between them. Other OMA enablers handle things outside the IETF's scope, such as client provisioning, out-of-band notification channels, and billing.

OMA names interfaces ME-1 and ME-2 for the client and server sides of the MEM protocol, ME-3 and ME-4 for out-of-band server and client interfaces, and ME-5 for managing server settings, user preferences and filters. The I2 label marks interfaces the MEM enabler does not specify.

The MEM server fronts an email server, which may be packaged with it or separate. OMA also allows MEM proxies ahead of firewalls and several deployment cases in which the client, proxy, MEM server and email server sit in different domains, such as a mobile operator, a third-party provider or an email service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone has an email app, which talks to a helper server, which talks to the real mailbox. Extra side channels carry things like alerts and setup.

sections.title: The LEMONADE Architecture and Its Mapping
sections.content:
The LEMONADE profile assumes an IMAP store (RFC 3501 with LEMONADE extensions) and a SUBMIT server (RFC 4409 with extensions), each connected to an MTA over ESMTP (RFC 5321). The mail client is a LEMONADE-aware Mail User Agent (MUA), and server-to-client notifications use external mechanisms outside LEMONADE's scope.

Mapped onto OMA, the MEM server and email server are logically combined. ME-2 splits into two interfaces: ME-2a is IMAP extended per the LEMONADE profile, and ME-2b is SUBMIT extended per the profile. The MUA is part of the MEM client, and the external notification mechanism is part of the OMA enablers.
sections.plainLanguage: Reading mail and sending mail use two existing email doors, each given a few extra phone-friendly tricks. Together they play the part of the helper server.

sections.title: Non-LEMONADE Back Ends
sections.content:
OMA does not require LEMONADE-compliant servers. For IMAP and SUBMIT servers without the LEMONADE extensions, a LEMONADE MEM enabler server sits in front and speaks plain IMAP and SUBMIT to them on the I2 interface.

For back ends that are not IMAP at all, such as POP3 servers or proprietary message stores, I2 designates proprietary adapters. The RFC stresses these figures are schematic and do not dictate implementation: the enabler may be collocated with the submit server, and it is deliberately labeled neither an IMAP proxy nor an IMAP back-to-back user agent.
sections.plainLanguage: If the mailbox behind the helper is an older kind, the helper translates for it. How it does that is left to the builder.

sections.title: Filters and Notifications
sections.content:
OMA stresses server-to-client notifications of email events, and filtering. LEMONADE defines four categories of filters:

  • AF, administrative filters, usually set by the provider for policies such as content filtering, virus protection and spam filtering.
  • DF, deposit filters, run when new email arrives. They can be Sieve filters (RFC 5228), including vacation notices (RFC 5230).
  • VF, view filters, which define which emails are visible to the MUA, done through IMAP.
  • NF, notification filters, which define for which server events an out-of-band notification is sent to the client.

The RFC leaves implementation and management of each to the referenced documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Filters are sorting rules at different stages: the provider's safety checks, sorting when mail arrives, choosing what you see, and choosing what makes your phone beep.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC lists security risks tied to out-of-band notifications, server configuration by the client, client configuration by the server, MEM proxy servers, MEM servers acting as intermediaries, and the measures used to traverse firewalls. It does not analyze them itself and refers readers to the relevant Internet Mail, IMAP, SUBMIT and LEMONADE documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo points out the places where trouble could sneak in and says to read the other documents for the fixes.
